posts.title: Why a Diamond Ring?
slides: WHY A DIAMOND RING?
Young: "Every proposal I've heard about comes with a diamond ring. Has it always been that way?"
Old: "In the 1930s, only about one in ten engagement rings held a diamond. Sales were slow, so in 1938 the diamond company De Beers hired an ad agency, N.W. Ayer."
Old: "In 1947, a copywriter named Frances Gerety wrote a line for them: 'A Diamond Is Forever.' It ran in De Beers ads from 1948."
Old: "The line kept running. By the century's end, about eight in ten engagement rings held a diamond, and in 1999 Advertising Age named it the slogan of the century."
Old: "Today the same line still helps sellers of natural diamonds stand apart from lab-grown ones. Whoever sells the ring benefits from the story that comes with it."

Which of your own traditions do you think began as a slogan?

Follow for more.

sources.item: De Beers, N.W. Ayer 1938, slogan 1947, ads from 1948, 10% to 80% diamond share, Advertising Age 1999

posts.title: Why So Busy?
posts.topic: A calendar with every square filled in
slides: WHY SO BUSY?
I once kept a calendar with every square filled in. Each square had a reason, yet I couldn't tell you what the whole month was for.
Somewhere along the way, we learned to answer "How are you?" with "Busy." It sounds like an achievement, so we keep saying it.
Ask who gains when your days are full. A packed calendar leaves little time to wonder what you would choose if the squares were empty.
Tomorrow, try leaving one square empty on purpose. Notice what you reach for when nothing is expected of you.

What would you put in an empty square?

slides: The glass baking dish
posts.caption:
The first glass baking dishes were borosilicate, made to take sudden heat. Many sold today are cheaper soda-lime glass that handles it less well. Would you move yours from fridge to oven?

#OldCrow #Baking #Cookware

posts.title: Who taught you the date on the carton is the day it spoils?
posts.topic: Best-before dates on food as a spoil date

slides.text: Who taught you the date on the carton is the day it spoils?
slides.scene: Medium shot of the old raven alone in a warm, lamp-lit home kitchen at evening, standing at an open refrigerator. He holds a small plain unbranded yogurt carton close, tilting it to study the small printed date on the lid with a calm, curious, slightly amused expression. Fridge shelves behind him hold plain unlabeled jars and vegetables. Warm golden light. No readable text, no logos.

posts.caption:
There's a moment most of us know: the yogurt says yesterday, and it goes in the bin before anyone looks inside.

Most of those dates were never about safety. In the US, the only date food law requires is the one on infant formula. A "best if used by" date is the maker's or the store's estimate of when the food tastes its best. Canada works much the same way: best-before dates are about quality, and true expiration dates are kept for a short list of things like meal replacements and nutritional supplements.

The FDA estimates that confusion over these labels accounts for about a fifth of the food thrown away at home. That's groceries someone worked hours to pay for.

The old raven still respects his fridge. Food that's been stored well should stay good past a best-before date, and food that has spoiled goes out, whatever the label says. He just likes to know what a number means before he lets it decide for him.

What's the last thing you threw out only because of the date?

#OldCrow #FoodWaste #ZeroWaste
